entries.title: The notebook as a way of thinking
entries.description: On unfinished thoughts, attention, and why a notebook should be more than storage.

source.text: Demonstration source note: this sample essay was written for the prototype. Replace it with your own words and sources when preparing real writing.
source.label: In the margin

question.text: The companion note develops the woodpecker question as a small exercise in looking closely.
question.label: In the margin

workbench.text: Leave an idea visible for a day. It may ask a better question the second time you pass it.
workbench.label: A small experiment

loose.text: Connections can be useful before they become explanations.
loose.label: A loose thread

content.text: Illustrative sample writing for exploring this website.

For a long time, I thought a notebook was somewhere to keep an idea safe. A sentence arrived; I wrote it down. A useful observation appeared; I gave it a page. The book filled slowly, and I felt that something had been accomplished.

But keeping a thought is different from working on it. When I returned to those pages, many of the sentences seemed complete only because I had stopped asking questions. The notebook had preserved the first version of an idea, including all the things I had failed to notice.
Give a thought somewhere to go
I am beginning to think of a notebook as
a workbench rather than a cupboard

. A place to put something unfinished where I can turn it around. A drawing can interrupt an argument. A question can remain a question for a while. Two unrelated observations can share a page without being forced into a conclusion.

The important part is the return. A page becomes interesting when the person reading it is no longer quite the person who wrote it. A week is sometimes enough. A conversation, a failed attempt, or an afternoon making something with my hands can change the meaning of an old sentence.
A good page does not only remember what I thought. It gives me a reason to think again.
Keep the edges open

This changes the kind of things worth writing down. Not only conclusions, but the small instructions that might lead somewhere: look at the underside; draw the joint again; find out how the woodpecker’s tongue works.
There is room here for an essay, a diagram, an unfinished object, and a note that turns out to be wrong. They do not need to agree yet. Their closeness may be the useful thing.

A later addition: leaving something visible is not the same as attending to it. I need a small habit of returning—a date in the diary, a question in the margin, or simply the decision to open the notebook before opening another tab.
What I want from this notebook is not an archive that proves I have been thinking. I want a practice that changes what I notice when I leave the page.

entries.title: A thought in two shapes
entries.description: A circle, a square, and the questions that appear where they meet.

drawing.text: The latest published sketch also appears in the homepage margin.

content.text: Illustrative sample writing for exploring this website.

attrs.alt: A cobalt circle and square overlap, crossed by pale diagonals and dotted axes, with a small arrow and hand-drawn marks.
attrs.caption: Study 01 · A thought in two shapes. Original geometric drawing made for this prototype.

content.text: The circle offers one kind of boundary; the square offers another. Neither is more complete. The interesting part is what becomes visible when they share the same centre.
I drew the diagonals last. They make the centre feel like an answer, although the drawing began as a question. Next time I might leave them out.
A drawing does not always need to illustrate a thought that already exists. Sometimes it is how the thought arrives.

practice.text: This note connects back to the essay about notebooks and forward to the sketch about two shapes.
practice.label: Try this

content.text: Illustrative sample writing for exploring this website.
I like a question that is small enough to carry in a pocket. Not “How does nature work?” but “What happens when this particular bird reaches into a tree?”
The smaller question asks something more useful of me. It asks me to look, sketch, read, and admit what I cannot yet explain. It gives attention a direction without promising an answer.
Today’s version of the exercise: choose one ordinary thing and describe it without reaching for a general lesson.
Start with what can be seen.
Draw the part that is difficult to describe.
Write down the next question, not a conclusion.
A handle. A hinge. The way a leaf joins its stem. There are enough questions within reach for a lifetime.

entries.title: A place for the unfinished
entries.description: Some things need to stay on the workbench a little longer.

waiting.text: Unfinished is not the same as abandoned. The difference may be attention.
waiting.label: Still taking shape

content.text: Illustrative sample writing for exploring this website.
There is a particular relief in putting a half-made thing down without putting it away. The next step can remain a little uncertain while the work stays visible.
I used to read that uncertainty as a failure of discipline. Sometimes it is. But sometimes the unfinished part is telling me where the interesting question begins.
The distinction may be whether I return. An unfinished thing that I keep meeting can become a conversation. An unfinished thing that I carefully hide becomes an excuse.
For now, I am leaving a small space on the desk for work that has not decided what it wants to be.

entries.title: On doing one thing slowly
entries.description: A study in repetition, feedback, and the useful limits of a small task.

feedback.text: A useful note records the conditions too: what changed, what stayed the same, and what is still uncertain.
feedback.label: On the bench

content.text: Illustrative sample writing for exploring this website.
A small task has an advantage over a grand intention: it can answer back. Draw the same curve ten times and the tenth curve knows something the first did not. The paper makes the difference visible.

Speed can hide this conversation. I finish the gesture before I have noticed which part of it needs attention. Slowing down does not make the work meaningful by itself, but it lets the feedback arrive.
A modest practice
Choose one gesture that takes less than a minute.
Repeat it until a difference becomes visible.
Change one thing, and notice what follows.

The point is not to perform patience. The point is to make a change small enough to understand. A line that wavers, a tool that catches, a sentence that refuses to settle: each offers a particular kind of information.
Work at a speed where you can still hear what the material is telling you.
This is another reason to keep a notebook nearby. The page can catch the observation before I turn it into a rule. “This worked today” is often more honest than “This is how it works.”
A finished object may be the result. A more careful way of noticing may be the thing I keep.
